source.title: Response-Based Knowledge Distillation for Multilingual Jailbreak Prevention Unwittingly Compromises Safety
source.authors: Max Zhang; Derek Liu; Kai Zhang; Joshua Franco; Haihao Liu

record.tranche_reason: Tests whether safety-related fine-tuning can worsen harmful-prompt outcomes, using response-based distillation on multilingual harmful prompts paired with safe teacher refusals rather than the original studies’ fine-tuning recipes.
record.gate_note: The study measures harmful-response rates after fine-tuning on teacher-generated safe refusals. This is not fine-tuning on harmful compliant examples, ordinary benign instruction data, or a test of token-position concentration, opening-prefill bypasses, or safety localization in weights. It reports a boundary-data classification and a simple-refusal data-purification experiment; the latter's JSR outcomes are included. GSM8K reasoning results, invalid-response rates, cited findings, and the boundary classification counts are not rows because they do not measure the harmful-compliance behavior named by the versions.
record.test_reason: The study fine-tunes safety-trained instruct models on non-harmful data (o1-mini safe refusals to XSafety prompts). It then measures harmful compliance (JSR on MultiJail) against the untuned models. This bears directly on V2, in a new setting: multilingual, response-based distillation of refusal data rather than ordinary instruction data. No other version is measured.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors conclude that response-based distillation of safe refusals increased JSR for all students, up to 16.6 pp. They concede the Llama-3-8B increase is not statistically significant across seeds. They attribute the degradation to boundary data, teacher-vulnerability amplification and catastrophic forgetting. Removing boundary refusals mitigates the safety loss (Gemma) or reverses it (Llama, Qwen), while reasoning loss persists.
record.recipe_differences: Response-based knowledge distillation with LoRA: approximately 28,190 harmful multilingual prompts are paired with o1-mini safe refusal responses, then used for two-epoch fine-tuning. This is not fine-tuning on compliant harmful examples or ordinary benign instruction data.
record.method_sensitivity: Outcome varies by model and training data: Gemma shows larger full-distillation increases; simple-refusal-only data reverses the JSR increase for Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-8B but not Gemma-2-2B-IT. The paper also reports model- and language-dependent outcomes.

fits_no_version.finding: Llama-3-8B's 'safe' rate drops significantly (77.3→73.4% mean), with rises in invalid rather than unsafe outputs. Separately, GSM8K reasoning falls in all models.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Benign or safety fine-tuning degrades coherence and capabilities even when harmful compliance does not rise.

record.problems: The authors note reliance on response-based black-box KD, a study focused mainly on models with 8B or fewer parameters (larger-model ablations extend to 14B), and reliance on a single primary LLM judge. The Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct overall JSR increase is statistically insignificant. Some language-wise results are described as marginal and correspond to roughly 5–10 prompts.
record.rows_left_out: No eligible harmful-compliance JSR results were omitted. GSM8K reasoning outcomes, invalid-response rates, judge-reliability comparisons, and boundary-refusal classification counts are not rows for the claim versions.

untested.parts: Ordinary benign instruction data (e.g., Alpaca/Dolly-style). Small data sizes (a few to a few hundred examples; this study uses ~28k). English-only setting.
No fine-tuning on harmful compliant examples.
No per-token KL or position analysis.
No prefilling, suffix or decoding attacks.
LoRA is used only as a training tool; there is no localization test.
The causal story (boundary data, vulnerability transfer, forgetting) concerns degradation, not why safety is shallow. It is mostly argued, not tested.

missing.what: Hyperparameter ablation: epochs 1–5 and learning rates 1e-5 to 2e-4 all gave similar JSR increases and no net safety gain. This is stated in words only, with no numbers.
Qwen3-8B unsafe rate rises in the unseen languages sw/jv as invalid responses fall (~10%). Llama shows ~3% JSR decreases there. Per-language values appear only in figures.

record.verdict_notes: The training data is safety refusal data paired with harmful prompts. It is benign in the sense of containing no harmful compliance, but it is not 'ordinary' instruction data, so the V2 link is by analogy to Qi et al.'s benign-data result, which the authors cite. Several rows are from single representative runs; only the overall JSRs for the three main models have multi-seed statistics. The evaluation relies on a single GPT-4o judge, which grades harsher than humans. The paper is not an original source.

versions.untested_parts: The training targets are safe refusals, not harmful compliant examples; it does not test fine-tuning on a few to a few hundred harmful examples.

It tests response-based distillation using safe refusals to harmful prompts, not ordinary benign instruction data or the original range of a few to a few hundred examples; the distillation set has ∼28,190 prompts.
No per-token KL or aligned-versus-base response-position measurement.
No compliant-opening prefills, suffix attacks, or decoding-change tests.
LoRA is used for fine-tuning, but the study does not test whether a small set of weights or ranks carries safety behaviour.
The study proposes boundary data, vulnerability transfer, and forgetting as explanations for safety degradation, but does not test why safety is shallow or first-token concentrated.
No training designed to spread safety beyond initial response tokens, or test of whether such deepening holds up.

relationships.condition: Gemma-2-2B-IT (LoRA and full SFT), Qwen3-8B, Llama-2-13b-chat, Gemma-3-12B-IT, with full refusal-distillation data
relationships.reason: JSR rises after fine-tuning on safe refusals. Gemma-2-2B goes 5.0→~19.7–21.6 (p≪0.0001) and Qwen3-8B goes 5.7→8.6 (p≪0.0001). Larger models rise too: Llama-2-13B by +8.4 pp, Gemma-3-12B by +6.8 pp (R5–R12, R16–R18).
relationships.display_finding: Jailbreak success rose from 5.0 to about 19.7–21.6 for Gemma-2-2B and from 5.7 to 8.6 for Qwen3-8B (both p≪0.0001), and by 8.4 points for Llama-2-13B and 6.8 points for Gemma-3-12B.

relationships.condition: Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct and Qwen3-14B with full distillation data

relationships.display_finding: Llama-3-8B rose a non-significant 1.4 points overall (p≈0.73) with tiers barely moving, and Qwen3-14B rose only 0.85 points with no uncertainty reported, so erosion is model-dependent.

relationships.condition: Training only on 'simple' refusals (boundary refusals removed)
relationships.reason: JSR falls below baseline for Llama-3-8B (12.5→5.9) and Qwen3-8B (5.7→4.03). Gemma-2-2B's rise is halved (to 11.96). Erosion depends on data composition (R13–R15).
relationships.display_finding: Training only on simple refusals, with boundary refusals removed, pushed JSR below baseline for Llama-3-8B (12.5 to 5.9) and Qwen3-8B (5.7 to 4.03) and halved Gemma-2-2B's rise (to 11.96), so erosion depends on data composition.
